title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, we won’t.
In this analysis, I look at total commuters (travel time table) across counties in Massachusetts (MA), and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Commuting data (and derivatives of it like ridership information) can dictate where funding goes for transportation infrastructure. This impacts not only a rider’s commute to work, but how they get anywhere in their community.

my_variable <- "B08303_001"

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

We can sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                             estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                               <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Dukes County, Massachusetts          8569   846    9.87
 2 Nantucket County, Massachusetts      7068   400    5.66
 3 Franklin County, Massachusetts      29787   730    2.45
 4 Berkshire County, Massachusetts     53440  1303    2.44
 5 Hampshire County, Massachusetts     64314  1441    2.24
 6 Barnstable County, Massachusetts    94875  1658    1.75
 7 Hampden County, Massachusetts      191547  2409    1.26
 8 Suffolk County, Massachusetts      354342  3887    1.10

10 Plymouth County, Massachusetts     229969  2460    1.07


Dukes County is the least reliable county. It has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate (calculated as moe_pct) of 9.87%.

text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 7 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     9
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            4


Originally when I had “high confidence” as moe_pct < 5, almost all the counties (12 of 14) fell into that category. Because of this, I changed the variable split to be:
moe_pct < 5 ~ “High confidence”
moe_pct < 10 ~ “Moderate”
This gave a more distributed split of 9 high confidence, 4 moderate, and 1 low confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                             myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                             <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 25001 Barnstable County, Massachusetts  94875   1658 230073    NA
2 25003 Berkshire County, Massachusetts   53440   1303 128047    NA
3 25005 Bristol County, Massachusetts    257154   2658 578436    NA
4 25007 Dukes County, Massachusetts        8569    846  20751    NA
5 25009 Essex County, Massachusetts      353800   3156 807258    NA
6 25011 Franklin County, Massachusetts    29787    730  70922    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now we can compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         12        579779.
2 Moderate                 2         17525 


The average population of high-confidence counties (579779 people) is higher than the average population of moderate counties (17525 people). A general pattern seems to be that the higher the population of a county, the more lower its margin of error.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The data we are looking at comes from the ACS, which is a sample. The smaller the place, the smaller the sample we’ll be able to get. Both Nantucket and Duke County consists of small islands off the southeastern coast of Massachusetts. Nantucket has an estimated population of 14299 and Duke County has an estimated 20751. Compared to Middlesex County with an estimated population of 1622896, it is not surprising that the communities we know the least about are Nantucket and Dukes County. They have the largest margin of error percentages (moe_pct), 5.66% and 9.87% respectively. This is at least 2.19% more than the next largest moe_pct and almost 5% more than Middlsex County, which has the smallest moe_pct. This is in part because of how small Nantucket and Duke County are.
Treating every county’s number as equally certain ignores differences in population, size, community context, and more. If a MA state agency were to allocate funding using the total estimate for travel time to work in the ACS, it would affect each county differently. In this analysis, Nantucket and Duke County could be negatively affected because of how different they are from the rest of Massachusetts. In addition, Nantucket and Dukes County are popular summer vacation spots. The significant summer tourism can impact commute times, both in how long it takes someone to get to work and also what work they are doing. In the off-season, residents may have to travel off-island for work. This requires either a plane or ferry ride, as there are no bridges that connect to either county’s islands. Nantucket and Dukes County residents have to deal with this unconventional commute year-round. The census does not take this into consideration.
We cannot do right by our communities if we take numbers only at face value.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
text:
Journalists, agencies, and advocacy organizations publish claims about neighborhood change all the time. Most of those claims rest on American Community Survey (ACS) estimates. Very few of them report margins of error, test whether a change is statistically detectable, or acknowledge what the data cannot support.
In this assignment, I verify claims about poverty rates and median household income in Philadelphia neighborhoods.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
section: The Article and What It Claims
text:
The Article and What It Claims
Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018. https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/
This article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims about poverty rates and median household income in Philadelphia neighborhoods.

**“the city’s** formidable 26 percent poverty rate”
“Fairhill in North Philadelphia registered a stunning 61 percent poverty rate.”
The “neighborhood of Eastwick in Southwest Philadelphia, near Philadelphia International Airport, showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community, rocketing from 12 percent during 2006-10 to 26 percent in the newest survey.”
White poverty throughout much of the city skyrocketed, led by the Northeast neighborhood of Holmesburg, which went from a 2 percent poverty rate to 19 percent.
The median household income of Tioga-Nicetown plummeted from $28,026 to $17,493, the largest drop in the city.

title: Assignment 3 - Verify the Claim
text:
Part 2 - Testing the Data
Second, we’ll test the data to see if it’s statistically significant or not.
Calculate the poverty rate for each tract and its margin of error. The poverty rate is the percentage of a population whose household income falls below the poverty line, which is set by the government and change by year. The census provides us with the information to be able to calculate this.


Code
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = 100 * pop_below_poverty_lineE / total_pop_pov_universeE
  )

# drop NA rows
philly_tracts_2010 <- na.omit(philly_tracts_2010)

# do the same for the other dataframe
philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = 100 * pop_below_poverty_lineE / total_pop_pov_universeE
  )

# drop NA rows
philly_tracts_2017 <- na.omit(philly_tracts_2017)

# taking a peek at the data on a map
ggplot(philly_tracts_2010) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_rate), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Poverty Rate In Philadelphia Tracts, ACS 2006-2010 5-Year Estimates",
       fill = NULL)









Calculate the margin of error. The margin of error gibes us a plus-or-minus range. This tells us how much the census survey results may differ from the views of the population. Remember that the ACS is a sample!


Code
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    moe_prop = moe_prop(pop_below_poverty_lineE, total_pop_pov_universeE, pop_below_poverty_lineM, total_pop_pov_universeM)
  )

philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    moe_prop = moe_prop(pop_below_poverty_lineE, total_pop_pov_universeE, pop_below_poverty_lineM, total_pop_pov_universeM)
)


Compute the coefficient of variation and flag reliability. The coefficient of variation measures the reliability of the data. High reliability (green circle) suggests high precision and consistency in the data (we want this!). Medium reliability (yellow circle) is typically sufficient for general use. Low reliability (red circle) reflects very low trustworthiness. As you’ll see below, the majority of the tracts’ poverty rate have a high reliability.


Code
# drop geometries 
philly_tracts_2010 <- philly_tracts_2010 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() 

philly_tracts_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() 

# calculate cv and make reliability table
reliability_table_2017 <- philly_tracts_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = case_when(TRUE ~ 100 * (moe_prop / 1.645) / poverty_rate),
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(cv) ~ NA_character_,
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    dot,
    NAME,
    moe_prop,
    poverty_rate,
    cv,
    flag
  )


reliability_table_2017 %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(moe_prop, poverty_rate),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = cv,
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "GEOID",
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Name",
    moe_prop = "Margin of error",
    poverty_rate = "Poverty rate (%)",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = c(dot, cv, flag)
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Population Below 100% of the Poverty Level",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia Tracts, ACS 2013–2017 5-year estimates"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable."
  ) %>%

Here, I join the tables together since I start to compute change between the two periods of time.
Compute the change between the two periods and the margin of error of that change. In order to refute or back up the claims made in the article, we need to look at the change between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 in a statistical manner.


Code
# join tables
philly_tract_combined <- left_join(philly_tracts_2017, philly_tracts_2010, by = "GEOID")

#calculating diff in pov rate
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(diff_poverty_rate = poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x)

# calculating standard error
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(SE2010 = (moe_prop.y*100)/1.645) %>%
  mutate(SE2017 = (moe_prop.x*100)/1.645)

# calculating standard error difference
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(SE_diff = sqrt((SE2010^2) + (SE2017^2)))

# calculating z-scores
philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(z_score = ((poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x)/SE_diff))

philly_tract_combined <- philly_tract_combined %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate.y-poverty_rate.x,
    se_1     = (moe_prop.y*100) / 1.645,
    se_2     = (moe_prop.x*100) / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

# visualize with error bars
philly_tract_combined %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  mutate( NAME.x = str_remove(NAME.x, " Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME.x, diff_poverty_rate), y = diff_poverty_rate)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = diff_poverty_rate > 0)) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change - SE_diff,
                      ymax = change + SE_diff), width = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 4)) +
    labs(title = "Statistically Significant Change in Poverty Rate",
         subtitle = "2013–2017 vs 2006–2010, ACS 5-year estimates for Philadelphia tracts",
         x = NULL, y = "Change in people below poverty level")

text:
Part 4 - Rewriting One of the Article’s Central Paragraph
Fairhill is the poorest neighborhood in Philly. It has an estimated poverty rate of 63.36% with a margin of error of 11.76%. The median household income is estimated to be $13,353 with a margin of error of $3,905. These seem like very alarming figures. However, this did not happen overnight and it doesn’t necessarily reflect the trajectory of the entire city. Historically, Fairhill was a very industrial part of Philly, a manufacturing hub anchored by Germantown Avenue. To lower cost, manufacturing jobs eventually moved away from the city or even overseas. According to Crossroads Philly, it was this economic collapse that has laid the conditions of what we call Fairhill today. While the statistic that Fairhill (or at least an estimation of the census tracts that make it up) has an alarmingly high poverty rate, we must look at it with context.
